outline.chapter_title: The Era of 1‑bit LLMs: Motivation and Overview
outline.description: Introduces the compute, memory, and energy bottlenecks of full‑precision LLMs and positions BitNet b1.58 as a practical, high‑performance ternary alternative. Summarizes the paper’s core claims, contributions, and why 1.58‑bit (ternary) weights can match FP16 models starting from medium scales.
subtopics: Scaling challenges of FP16/BF16 LLMs: cost, latency, power, and deployment barriers
Post‑training quantization (PTQ) trend (16→4 bits) and its limitations
From binary/1‑bit models to ternary: what 1.58 bits means (values in {-1, 0, +1})
Why zeros matter: feature filtering and reduced interference
BitNet lineage and the move from multiplications to integer additions
Key contributions of BitNet b1.58: accuracy parity with FP16 from 3B, large efficiency gains
High‑level benefits: latency, memory, throughput, and energy improvements
Roadmap of the textbook and how chapters build from foundations to systems and results

outline.description: Builds the theory and practice of quantization needed to understand b1.58. Covers weight/activation quantization, straight‑through estimation, and the specific absmean ternary quantizer used in the paper.
subtopics: Quantization taxonomy: uniform vs non‑uniform; per‑tensor vs per‑channel; zero‑point vs symmetric
Backprop through discrete variables: Straight‑Through Estimator (STE) basics
Absmean scaling for weights: gamma = mean(|W_ij|); RoundClip to {-1, 0, +1}
Quantization error sources: clipping vs rounding; role of zero in reducing error propagation
Activation quantization in b1.58: 8‑bit, per‑token scaling to [-Qb, Qb]; removal of zero‑point
Contrast with prior PTQ methods (SmoothQuant, GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP/QuIP‑Sharp)
Implications of symmetric activations and no pre‑nonlinearity [0, Qb] scaling
Numerical stability considerations in ternary quantization

outline.description: Details how BitNet replaces dense linear layers with BitLinear to exploit ternary weights and 8‑bit activations. Explains LLaMA‑alike design choices that maximize compatibility and performance.
subtopics: Transformer recap: attention and MLP blocks; where matmuls dominate cost
BitLinear in place of nn.Linear: integer additions, sign flips (×−1), and zero skips (×0)
Where BitLinear is applied: attention projections, MLP layers
LLaMA‑alike components: RMSNorm, SwiGLU, rotary positional embeddings (RoPE), no biases
Precision layout: 1.58‑bit weights, 8‑bit activations; embeddings kept in full precision
KV‑cache considerations with 8‑bit activations
Kernel and software stack: 2‑bit Ladder kernel; FasterTransformer; Hugging Face, vLLM, llama.cpp compatibility
System‑friendliness: simple symmetric scaling and zero‑point removal

outline.description: Covers end‑to‑end training practices for b1.58, contrasting them with post‑training quantization. Discusses data, token budgets, stability tricks, and evaluation protocols used in the paper.
subtopics: From‑scratch quantization‑aware training vs PTQ for LLMs
Data and scale used in the paper: RedPajama, 100B tokens for pretraining
Activation scaling per token to [-Qb, Qb] and its stability benefits
STE through ternary weight quantization; maintaining effective scales with absmean gamma
Why RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and removing biases help stability in low‑bit regimes
Mixed‑precision training pipeline and implementation notes
Validation metrics and benchmarks: perplexity (WikiText‑2, C4), zero‑shot tasks via lm‑evaluation‑harness
Practical training checklist: initialization, gradient clipping, logging, and ablations to consider

outline.chapter_title: Systems and Hardware Efficiency of Ternary LLMs
outline.description: Explains why 1.58‑bit LLMs run faster and cooler. Connects arithmetic, memory hierarchy, and kernel design to observed latency, memory, and throughput improvements.
subtopics: Arithmetic paradigm shift: replacing FP16 mul/add with INT additions and sign flips
Energy model recap: FP16 add/mul vs INT8 add; 71.4× matmul energy reduction on 7nm (paper’s estimate)
Memory hierarchy: DRAM↔SRAM bandwidth as a bottleneck; weight‑transfer savings with ternary
Latency sources during inference and why time per output token drops
Scaling behavior: larger models amplify BitLinear benefits as matmul share grows
Throughput and batch sizing under memory limits; pipeline parallelism on 2×A100 80GB (LLaMA‑70B baseline)
Kernel considerations: 2‑bit Ladder kernel, zero‑point removal simplifies implementation
Deployment notes: quantized KV caches, stream scheduling, and operator fusion opportunities

outline.chapter_title: Empirical Results: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Scaling
outline.description: Summarizes the paper’s quantitative findings across perplexity, zero‑shot tasks, latency, memory, throughput, and energy. Highlights where b1.58 matches or surpasses FP16 baselines.
subtopics: Accuracy parity from 3B+: b1.58 matches FP16 perplexity starting at 3B (WikiText‑2, C4)
Zero‑shot tasks: ARC‑Easy/Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, OpenBookQA, BoolQ; performance gap narrows with scale
3B scale: 2.71× faster, 3.55× less GPU memory vs FP16 baseline (paper)
3.9B vs FP16‑3B: 2.4× faster, 3.32× less memory, better end‑task performance (paper)
Larger models: 70B b1.58 is 4.1× faster than FP16 LLaMA baseline (paper)
Energy: majority ops shift to INT8 adds; end‑to‑end energy advantage grows with model size
Throughput on 2×A100 80GB with seq=512: up to 11× larger batch, 8.9× higher throughput (paper)
Scaling tokens to 2T: b1.58‑3B outperforms StableLM‑3B on WinoGrande, PIQA, SciQ, LAMBADA, ARC‑Easy

outline.chapter_title: A New Cost–Performance Scaling Law and Design Playbook
outline.description: Presents the paper’s scaling equivalences and translates them into practical design guidance. Explains why ternary zeros improve modeling and how to choose model sizes under cost constraints.
subtopics: Stated equivalences: 13B (1.58‑bit) ≻ 3B (FP16); 30B (1.58‑bit) ≻ 7B (FP16); 70B (1.58‑bit) ≻ 13B (FP16) in latency/memory/energy
When b1.58 reaches accuracy parity: capacity threshold around 3B parameters
Feature filtering via zero weights: sparsity‑like benefits without explicit pruning
Pareto frontier shift: simultaneous gains in accuracy and efficiency
Embedding precision and activation bit‑width trade‑offs
Guidelines for selecting model size vs deployment budget (latency, memory, energy)
When to prefer b1.58 training over 4‑bit PTQ for end‑to‑end cost and robustness
Interplay with sequence length and KV‑cache size in planning deployments

outline.description: Explores practical deployment domains and the broader ecosystem. Outlines open research problems and hardware co‑design opportunities suggested by the 1‑bit paradigm.
subtopics: Edge and mobile: CPU‑friendly integer operations; enabling larger on‑device models under tight power
Long‑context inference: 8‑bit activations halve KV‑cache cost; paths to 4‑bit or lower caches
Mixture‑of‑Experts synergy: reduced memory and inter‑chip communication overhead
Tooling: integrating b1.58 with Hugging Face, vLLM, llama.cpp, FasterTransformer; evaluation via lm‑evaluation‑harness
Hardware co‑design: beyond GPUs—specialized LPUs/accelerators optimized for ternary/integer adds
Kernel R&D: beyond 2‑bit Ladder kernels, operator fusion, memory‑bandwidth optimizations
Reproducibility and benchmarking practices for low‑bit LLMs
Ethical and environmental impact: lower energy per token and wider accessibility
